utterances.text: No. We did not receive any such information from the Corps Command because we were a long way away. Our communication with the command was made extremely difficult because of the combat operations that were ongoing in the broader area of Trnovo, so that we communicated via the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and it was very hard to establish communication in that way. Anyway, our communications were limited to the dispatch of regular combat reports, and we were suffering serious casualties and requiring materiel and equipment and other supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When did you come to the territory that was within the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps? I'm referring to the period of the beginning of July 1995, after the Srebrenica operation had already begun.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I was there only twice for brief periods. I mean, I would come from Treskavica or, rather, Trnovo, my assignment being to intervene with the Corps Commander General Zivanovic so that he should find a way for us to fill in our units with new personnel because we had very great losses ever since our arrival in the Trnovo area and throughout the time we spent in that area. We were exposed to very severe fire from the Muslim forces and the rapid deployment forces of the French battalion on Mount Igman. The morale in the unit of which I was a part at the time was seriously undermined. Perhaps for the first time during the war that I was confronted with such a situation in the units because of these high casualties, and that was the reason for me to go on the 12th of July, in the evening, to the Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Who did you find at the Corps Command in the evening of the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: The duty operations officer was Colonel Jocic. I briefly met with Commander Zivanovic, very briefly. Who else was there? I saw Major Pajic, several soldiers from the communications centre, and two of my associates from the press centre. I can't remember now whether there was anyone else that I saw then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Before we go back to your brief encounter with the Corps Commander General Zivanovic, did your associates from the press centre inform you of the situation in the press centre, the news, the current situation, and so on, the things that were important at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Since I was in a kind of vacuum as far as information was concerned, I asked my colleagues what was going on. They didn't know much. They couldn't tell me much because all the information for the public at large at that time went through the press centre of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. They only told me that during the day they had forwarded an appeal or a call, whatever you like to call it, to the local radio stations, asking companies, private haulers, to send their vehicles to Srebrenica for the transportation of the population towards Kladanj and Tuzla. That is what I learnt at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You said that you also spoke to the Corps Commander, General Zivanovic. What did you speak to him about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I briefed the commander on the situation in the territory I had come from. He did not make any promises about reinforcements, because he said he was short of forces, but he insisted that I go back immediately and that all of us who were in this mini command of the unit should be constantly with the fighters, that we should invest all the authority we could command to maintain the required level of combat readiness and morale, which, of course, we did upon our return. We were constantly with the fighting men on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This was on the 12th, in the evening, was it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber where you were on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I spent the night between the 12th and the 13th in the corps. I picked up some supplies that I needed to take with me for the command and the fighters, and in the morning of the 13th, sometime after breakfast or around breakfast time, I met with General Krstic, who just briefly asked me what was new. I briefed him, as I had the Corps Commander, and I received the same instructions from him as I had from General Zivanovic. But General Krstic also said that it would be a good thing if I could prepare some gifts, primarily cigarettes, for our wounded combatants who were undergoing treatment in the hospital of the Main Staff of the VRS at Sokolac, and that we should go and visit them together, as we had always done. I went to Sokolac a little before General Krstic, and we met at the Romanija Hotel at Sokolac around 11.30. From there, we went on to the Main Staff hospital. We spoke to the doctors and together visited our wounded soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say "the Main Staff hospital," does that mean the Drina Corps did not have its own hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: No. In the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps, there were three medical institutions where our fighters were treated, and that was the hospital of the Main Staff in Sokolac that was established at the beginning of the war, the hospital in Milici, and the hospital in Zvornik. We did not have a corps hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In the Main Staff hospital, in addition to the wounded from the Drina Corps, there were wounded from other units, weren't there; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. You have just reminded me. This hospital of the Main Staff played a very important role in the course of the war. The fighters from the whole territory of the eastern part of Republika Srpska were treated there, also civilians. Even Muslims were treated there, and in quite large numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say "the wounded," how many of them were there at the time, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: You mean our wounded?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I mean the wounded that you visited, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Well, you see, General Krstic and I, while we were together in the brigade, whenever we had an opportunity to do so, we would visit the wounded soldiers, and we never made any distinction as to whether he belonged to our units or units of the Sarajevo-Romanija or Herzegovina Corps. We would express encouragement to all of them, give them all the same gifts. And just then, on the 13th, there were about a hundred of them, I'm sure, in all the wards of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How long did this visit of yours to the hospital last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: The visit was completed by 1500 hours or thereabouts. We also managed to speak to the surgeons in the meantime. And upon the General's proposal, we called on my mother who lives in a village on the way to Han Pijesak. She lived alone, so we went to see her. She made us some lunch and we ate there. We stayed there for about an hour, approximately, an hour and a half. From there, we went to Han Pijesak, that is, we went to the village of Kusace where we visited General Krstic's in-laws at the parents of his wife. This is where we had coffee. I think I had a glass of plum brandy. I don't know whether the General did. From there -- it was already getting late in the afternoon -- we went to Krivaca, which is situated above Zepa, and the General told me that he had established a forward command post there. He also said that he would spend a few days there and that, from there, we will be able to have contact, that is, he would be able to have contact with me from there once I returned to Treskavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Who did you find at the Krivaca forward command post and what did it look like? Could you describe it for the Chamber? What is actually a forward command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: This forward command post would be established by way of a simple tent, and this is what I saw there. We had a cook there. I forgot the name of that woman. Amovic was also there, who was Commander of the Staff Command, a few soldiers. Whether Vicic, Colonel Vicic was there, I don't know. I saw him somewhere. I don't know if it was there or somewhere else, I can't remember, but I saw him sometime during the day. Maybe I saw him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: For a very short period of time. Krstic rushed me, telling me to go back, and once again he told me to spend time with the soldiers, to try and boost their morale, and once conditions are created, he said that he would come and that a rotation would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I went to Vlasenica. Actually, I first went to Han Pijesak to get some cigarettes for the fighters. They smoked so much. I wanted to take some cigarettes to them, to Trnovo. After that, I went to Vlasenica, took some hygiene supplies and some parcels that the parents of the combatants were sending them. I put it all in a Yugo vehicle which belonged to the press centre and went to Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Krstic remained at the Krivaca forward command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We didn't see each other again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And you don't know the whereabouts of General Krstic in the days that followed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: No. I don't know. We couldn't communicate. I was able to communicate with the corps but I couldn't reach him. We didn't even speak on the telephone. It was not possible at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber something about General Zivanovic and his stay -- and his visit to the Drina Corps? Did you have any contact with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Well, we were sending him combat reports on a regular basis, and we also received his instructions, the instructions that he had already once given. So he was repeating them. He said that we should try and stick it out, to be with the soldiers as much as possible, to serve as an example to them, because the commander of the corps was aware of our situation. He was aware of the serious losses that we had. But the contacts with him were not very frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many days after your stay there this was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: You mean the contacts with General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I think that we had contact until the 20th, as far as I can remember. It was actually him. He would call the communications centre at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and then his message would be forwarded to us. So that was the kind of contact that we had with him. It continued perhaps after the 20th. I don't know. I had a diary throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, I must admit that I feel somewhat lost in this testimony. The witness said that he had stayed two months or thereabouts at Trnovo. At least two times he came to the corps. Once it was on the 12th of July, and he described to us the day of the 12th of July and the 13th of July, but I don't know -- I still don't know anything about his second visit. Do you plan to cover that? Oh, yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was just about to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When was your -- when did your second visit take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: It took place sometime around the 23rd or 24th of July, but it was on a private basis. I went there for family reasons, and again I stayed two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Where exactly did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I went to the press centre, I went to see my mother. It was all in a rush.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness DA, you have known General Krstic for quite a while?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. I know General Krstic from our secondary school days. We used to be school colleagues. We went to the grammar school together and we graduated together. We finished at the same time. Once we left high school, Krstic went to the military academy and I studied languages, but we would see each other from time to time. And then for quite some time, for several years, we didn't see each other, up until the beginning of the war, and Fate wanted us to meet again in the same unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell something about General Krstic as an officer, since you spent quite some time in his vicinity during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: It is very difficult to me to separate the personality of General Krstic as a man and as an officer, because, Your Honours, you must understand: We went to school together; we were colleagues in the grammar school. Krstic has always been a great man, in my eyes, and he is also an honourable officer for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: While he was the brigade commander, you used to tour the lines that were held by your fighters together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. It happened very often, and I was always more than willing to do that. Now you just reminded me of Krstic's arrival in the VRS. To be quite frank, I was really glad to learn that he had arrived, because I knew, first of all, what his qualities as a man were. But I must say that, at the beginning of the war, our army was not yet organised properly. However, with the arrival of Krstic in the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, thanks to his reputation, thanks to his dedication and his tireless work, this unit became a powerful military community. You said that we used to tour our units together, and it is true; I was always quite impressed by the way soldiers were accepting General Krstic, who at that time was a lieutenant colonel. As time went by, he was more and more respected and liked, not only by the members of the VRS, by the members of our brigade, but also by the civilians, by the people. I remember just now how much effort he made in order to ensure transport for the displaced population from Olovo and how he managed to organise a bus line for those unfortunate people to be able to reach Sokolac, and it was all in the midst of war, to reach Sokolac to buy the basic supplies that they needed or to get medical help that they didn't have as refugees. There are many other examples of his correct attitude, not only towards the soldiers but also towards the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: During our conversation yesterday, when we were discussing your testimony here, you told me about something that happened in the autumn of 1993 involving Croatian soldiers. Could you briefly describe that event to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of the brigade was, during a certain period of time, very large, geographically speaking, so that our units -- some of our units were deployed in the vicinity of Vares. I believe that it was in the territory of the villages of Okruglice and Brgule.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Vares was under the control of the BH army and the Croatian Defence Council at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: The majority of the population in Vares in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina was Croat, and for quite some time the Croats had the upper hand in that town. However, when the conflict broke out, I mean the armed conflict between the HVO and the BH army, the entire Croat community from Vares left the town and fled to our territory, that is, to the villages that I have just mentioned, where our soldiers took them in and offered them protection. There were several thousands of Croats there, but, Your Honours, not only civilians, women and children, but also HVO soldiers. Many of them had been disarmed. However, there was still a significant number of them who still had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say that they had been disarmed, who had disarmed them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Members of the BH army. General Krstic engaged almost the complete -- all the members of the brigade and the staff, and he made sure that we assembled all in that area and offer help to those unfortunate people, and he personally spent days and hours trying to help them. All those who managed to reach our combat lines survived, were taken care of, were offered adequate medical help. And when they arrived in Sokolac, upon their wish, they were transported by us either to Yugoslavia or to the Western Bosnia via Duvno and Livno from where some of them eventually reached Kiseljak. Not long ago, I got a postcard from some people, greetings from some people in Australia who were there, greetings for both myself and General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The period of time you're referring to, the autumn of 1993. In that period of time, HVO had a contact line, a confrontation line, with the VRS in several areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility of our corps, we didn't have any major conflicts with them, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But that was the case in Posavina and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes, but that was very far from our area of responsibility, and I don't know much about it except what I could read in the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this may be a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I believe we should have a break at this point because we are working according to the same schedule as we did with General Krstic. So we will have a 15-minute break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic. You may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness DA, a moment ago, you told Their Honours that the hospital of the Main Staff in Sokolac treated, in addition to the wounded, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. civilian population. Tell me, in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Romanija Brigade for the duration of the war, which means from 1992 until the end of the war, were there localities, villages, settlements inhabited exclusively by Muslims? Could you tell Their Honours very briefly some data about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the war, that is, during the summer of 1992, in agreement with the local authorities, the army of Republika Srpska offered the Muslims that they should stay and continue living in their villages, in their own homes, guaranteeing them full security and normal living conditions on condition that they return the weapons. Many accepted this. Thus, for instance, the inhabitants of the villages of Vrhbarje and Burati stayed on in the area throughout the war. So did some other villages. Personally, I would be given orders by General Krstic to visit those people, to call on them to try, in agreement with the authorities -- and those were my duties according to establishment -- to provide them with health care and essential living needs. I'm thinking of food and everything else. We did so on a continuous basis. And anyway, this was registered by numerous TV crews. They recorded our encounters with those inhabitants. Sometimes I was even criticised by some people when I went to visit those villagers. Why did I exchange such cordial greetings with them, hugging them and so on? But all this was just normal. It was humane. Those Muslims sent gifts to General Krstic in the form of fruit; plums, apples, pears. So there was something that stood out as good among the general horror.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness DA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Visnjic. Witness DA, you will now answer questions put to you by Mr. Cayley. Mr. Cayley, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness DA. I'd just like to talk a little bit about your personal background. When did you do your military service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. In 1975 to 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And am I right in saying that, in 1992, you were mobilised, you volunteered to serve in the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I was mobilised like all other able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I think you've already said in your evidence that your position, your first position, was that of Deputy Commander for Morale, Legal, and Religious Affairs with the 2nd Romanija Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that is where you first encountered General Krstic; is that right? I realise you went to school with him when you were a boy, but in the VRS, that's when you first encountered him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes, after many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could have an exhibit, please, Exhibit 804.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, as you know, the VRS relied heavily on JNA regulations and rules in order to govern how military staff worked, and what I want to show you, very briefly, is the instructions. I think these are the instructions to the 4th Corps of the JNA on carrying out priority assignments in peacetime and wartime. And you can take a look at that document. Do you have the B/C/S -- do you have the Serbian version in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this document, General Krstic has already acknowledged, is a document that was used in the VRS, and I want to turn specifically to page 16, page 16 of the Serbian version, page 21 of the English version, which sets out the regulations on the Body for Moral Guidance and Legal Affairs in the corps. Now, with that explanation, what was the date that you moved from the 2nd Romanija Corps to the Body for Moral Guidance and Legal Affairs of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think, if I can refresh your memory, you said that you moved in June of 1994; isn't that right? June or July of 1994 you moved --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I don't know the exact date. It's written down in the military documents, but I didn't think it was important for me to remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, just looking at paragraph 3, you see it sets out the tasks for the Body for Moral Guidance and Legal Affairs. And if you go to -- I think it's line 5 in the Serb version, it says that "The Body's most important tasks are to monitor, analyse, plan, and organise moral education in subordinate units." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: On page 16?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges what that involved? You were an officer in the Body for Moral Guidance and Legal Affairs. What did you do to implement that regulation, as a member of the staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: As a member of the brigade command, I visited very frequently the units in the field; I monitored the situation with respect to morale; I spoke to the soldiers; I listened to all their requests, proposals; and did my best to resolve all the problems within my jurisdiction, if it was possible to do so. Of course, it was not always possible to resolve all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the next regulation which you can see, which states: "To take measures to protect commands and units from psychological propaganda activities by the enemy." Can you say what you did at both corps and brigade level in order to implement that regulation on your work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: We would convey to the fighting men in both units the truth, on the one hand, and what was not true, on the other, and which had been broadcast to the public by the other side. There were certain ill-intentioned reports in the foreign press. There were also malicious reports on the radio and on television. And anyway, as a journalist, I must say that sometimes I was critical of my colleagues who were not well informed and properly trained, and sometimes out of the best intentions they made major blunders, not knowing the situation properly and adequately. So sometimes we had to correct those errors, as far as it was possible to do that, by means of the radio, television, and talking to the soldiers, drawing their attention to the truth. You must understand that this was a period of very lively diplomatic activities on the part of both President Karadzic and all the political bodies that were in power at the time. There were the conferences in Lisbon, Geneva, London. All these different events needed to be described to each individual soldier in simple terms so that even those who didn't have adequate education would be able to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you recall the ill-intentioned reports or malicious reports in foreign press radio and television? Can you give the Judges any examples of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: My diary would mean a lot to me now. I can't remember just now, just this minute, but some of those reports were carried by our own media, not to mention what we had access to from the Muslim media, which we were able to monitor in view of the closeness of their transmitters, so that we could follow their programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues ...] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There were examples when the achievements of our units were underrated and the failures of the opposing side glorified. There were even some really funny situations, and sometimes they could turn ugly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you regard the Muslim media during the war as essentially biased and untruthful?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Of course. I remember before the combat operations began, during talks between party leaders, one of the demands was for the second programme of Sarajevo television at the time to be given to the Serbs for their use. However, that was never accepted. So you can imagine, and I said that moment ago, what a handicap that was for us in our efforts to present the truth and to fight for justice in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Whereas you, as a Serb officer, did your utmost to present a true picture of Serb army activities, Bosnian Serb army activities to the world?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I am, in the first place, a language expert and less an officer. I did write telling the truth. For me the truth was above all else. And I managed to do so to the extent to which circumstances allowed, and for that I am deeply grateful as a person and as a journalist to my colleagues from the third channel of French television, my colleagues from Greek TV studios, and some others for their sincerity with which they informed world public opinion, and particularly our colleagues from Japan, who also frequently reported from our areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, Witness, we could go back to the document. I want to take you to the next task that you had, which was to prepare, organise, and carry out psychological propaganda activities against enemy units. Can you explain to the Judges how you carried out psychological propaganda activities against enemy units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: We responded in equal measure, if we could, the same way the enemy treated us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you be more specific and explain to the Judges some of the measures that you took in order to, as it were, carry out this psychological propaganda on Bosniak units, Bosnian Muslim units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I said, and I keep repeating, that our handicap was the absence of adequate technical resources for all this. The Serb radio television at Pale was formed in a makeshift studio. There were only three good-quality reporters who came and were objectively qualified for the job, whereas the others were young men and women who were learning the trade of journalism in those difficult times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry. I've got to interrupt you. I think you may have misunderstood my question. What I want to know is the actual -- nothing -- I don't need to know about the technical shortages, material shortages. Can you just explain to the Judges the measures you in the Bosnian Serb army would take to carry out propaganda activities against enemy units.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I'll give you a concrete example. If, for instance, our lines would be moved forward at the expense of the enemy, on the enemy's side, the information media would deny that, and we would try, with the help of images and words, to show that that was not true, that we had the advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And naturally, if, for example, your -- I just need to read the transcript for a second.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, for example, the Bosnian Muslim army made inroads into Bosnian Serb army lines, naturally, you reported to the Bosnian Serb people that the Bosnian Muslim army had made successful advances on Bosnian Serb positions? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I do. You see, a war is a war. Sometimes we acknowledged and we sometimes didn't, fearing that this could affect combat morale, which is only logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So in essence, you did exactly the same thing as the Bosnian Muslims. You didn't always acknowledge when you had suffered defeats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: More often than they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've said in the course of your work that you had little or nothing, I think, to do with legal matters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. Very little, relatively speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you recall within the corps staff, in the Drina Corps staff, who was responsible for legal matters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: The assistant for moral and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would that be Lieutenant Colonel Cerovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes, while he was with the corps. But Mr. Cerovic was a sick man, so he would be on leave very often, that is, from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Cerovic, when you were in the Drina Corps, was your immediate superior within the staff branch of moral guidance and legal affairs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in the Main Staff of the Bosnian Serb army, the head of moral guidance and legal affairs within the VRS army was General Gvero; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Assistant, not the head. It is true that that was Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So he was the assistant chief for moral and legal affairs within the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: No. He was the Assistant Commander. Assistant to the Commander of the VRS for moral, religious, and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. These titles I know are very important to get absolutely correct. Now, if we just quickly finish with this document that's in front of us, which is the same one that you have --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And it moves down to the next section with the assistant commander for moral guidance and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the third section is: "To plan and supervise training to promote the moral education of soldiers and officers and to inform commands and units." Now, in supervising the training of moral education of soldiers and officers, did this involve instructing people in normal standards of good conduct as a soldier or an officer, civilised standards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And did your work involve teaching soldiers and officers about basic standards of behaviour in warfare towards civilian, towards prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. I had my own assistants for the same kind of affairs at the level of battalion, so it was through them that I was able to coordinate the work and to reach every single soldier, in the sense that you asked me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you just tell the Judges the kind of instruction that you gave to soldiers and officers about how they should conduct themselves during warfare, particularly with regard to civilians and prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Everything we did was based on the principles of the Geneva Conventions and the rules of service of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So it would be correct to say, based on what you're saying, that the VRS soldiers and officers throughout all the brigades were familiar with basic standards of conduct towards civilians and prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes, mostly. However, you must understand that the soldiers would be transferred very often. Many soldiers were killed in action or placed hors de combat. New soldiers would come to take their place, very often refugees from Central Bosnia or from Sarajevo, whom we didn't manage to form, to educate in that sense, in a timely fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How did you go about instructing soldiers and officers on basic standards of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Through my assistants at the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did he give lectures, classes too, of the soldiers and officers on the subject?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was a war, and we couldn't find time for teaching. All we could do was to be in constant contact with the people and try to talk to them as much as possible, I mean with the people out there in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm not criticising the efforts that you made; I'm just trying to establish with you how you actually passed on to officers and soldiers these very basic standards of humanitarian law that apply in warfare. Am I correct in saying that you did this through one of the assistant commanders in the battalion, who would give basic instructions to soldiers and officers within your brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. You are right. However, I must say that we also tried to inform them through bulletins and magazines that we published whenever we could, and amidst all these pieces of information having to do with the front lines, we tried to present these aspects that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And was this a practice that was carried out throughout the Drina Corps; there were assistant commanders in all of the brigades of the Drina Corps, as far as you know, giving basic instruction in international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: That was done according to the establishment of each particular brigade and battalion. It was a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And all of this instruction throughout all the brigades was coordinated at the Drina Corps level; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Through the Main Staff, that is, from the Main Staff through corps, up until the level of individual units, basic units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So we can fairly say that throughout all of the corps of the VRS, some efforts were made to give basic instruction to soldiers and officers in basic standards of conduct in warfare?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes. Similarly, we would often discuss the matter with General Gvero, and we were trying to find possibilities, solutions to reach individual soldiers, though, as I have already indicated, it was very difficult, given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think you also said that a part of your job was to inform soldiers and officers within your brigade, and indeed when you went to the Drina Corps staff, about current affairs, world affairs that affected them, and I'd like to give you an exhibit which is in fact an indictment. It's Exhibit 805.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if you could help the witness, Mr. Usher, by giving him the version in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, just before I ask you a question, Witness, I think you said in your evidence that you had liaison contact with press agencies from all over the world: CNN you mentioned, Reuters; I think you mentioned some Japanese and French colleagues that you met. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you'll see that this is an indictment of Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic. Now, as you know, in July of 1995 Radovan Karadzic was the Commander-in-Chief of the VRS and Ratko Mladic was the Chief of Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Ratko Mladic was the Commander of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this indictment was confirmed and indeed published on the 25th of July of 1995, and you will probably recall that it made world news and, I believe, was transmitted on all of the news agencies that we've just mentioned. Can you explain to the Judges the effect that this had on the soldiers and officers within the Drina Corps when this indictment was made public?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Both President Karadzic and General Mladic enjoyed a great amount of respect both from the units of the VRS and the people in general. Everyone was surprised when they heard about the indictment, but the reaction was the same both by the people and by the soldiers; Why our commander? Why our president, rather than Alija, for example, referring to Alija Izetbegovic, and others who started the war. So that was basically the reaction of both the people and the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And when this indictment was made public, everybody within the Drina Corps, indeed everybody in the VRS, knew about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that everybody knew about it. It was quite difficult to have this amount of material made accessible to every single soldier at every single post.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But I'm right in saying that news of this indictment was transmitted by the likes of Reuters, CNN, other international news agencies with whom you had contacts as a public affairs officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Yes, of course the agencies transmitted the news, but what was the use of such broadcast for a soldier who didn't speak any other language but his mother tongue, the Serbian language, and for the soldiers who had perhaps only one small transistor in a far away trench somewhere in the mountains? It was enough for those people to have heard about the fact that their president, their commander, had been indicted. They were offended, because they believed in the justified cause of the fight of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you have to go out yourself as part of the body for moral and legal affairs and try and explain why this indictment had been made public, had been confirmed by the War Crimes Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: No. There was no need for me to do that nor did I have any orders to that effect. People didn't need much explanation. Their anger was huge because they were deeply convinced of the just cause of the struggle that they had been leading for four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in July of 1995, when this was published, you, I think -- were you still on the corps staff in July of 1995, on the Drina Corps staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: No. I was at Treskavica. So I didn't have the complete version of the indictment except for what I heard at the radio, that is, only portions of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you managed to discover this indictment, hear about this indictment, even though you were up in Treskavica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DA
utterances.text: Thanks to a transistor that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it's probably time for us to finish for the day, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You've called me McCayley before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But it is Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's a compliment, actually. We share an office, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be very flattered if I had an opportunity to christen you once again, to baptise you once again. We have spent quite some time with Mr. McCloskey. And we do need a break at this point. I should like to tell you that we will continue in the following fashion: We will be sitting tomorrow starting at twenty minutes past nine. Thank you very much, Witness, for coming here to testify. We have to have a break at this point in your testimony, but we will be back tomorrow to hear you again, and we will see you at twenty minutes past nine tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 3rd day of November, 2000 at 9.20 a.m.
